name: Upturn
description:
Upturn is a district that refuses to stop performing. The old Uptown entertainment district — home to the Aragon Ballroom, the Riviera Theatre, and a century of Chicago music history — was supposed to die when the floods came and the corporations redrew the map. The lakefront venues took water damage. The entertainment economy collapsed when people stopped going out and started jacking into neural entertainment feeds. The residential hotels that once housed the neighborhood's eclectic mix of immigrants, artists, and the marginally housed were condemned, cleared, or converted to data storage. Uptown should have become another Managed Decline Zone, another name on the list of places the city used to have.

But the stages wouldn't close. The Aragon — that impossible Moorish fantasy of a building, its terra cotta facade cracked and patched with industrial sealant — reopened as an unlicensed neural entertainment venue within two years of the last official show. The Riviera became a black-market performance space where musicians, storytellers, and experience-chip artists perform for audiences who are tired of corporate-curated content. The entertainment economy didn't die. It went underground, went gray, went weird. Upturn's venues now host something that doesn't have a clean name: live performance enhanced by neural interface technology, where the audience doesn't just watch the show but feels it, transmitted directly through their implants by performers who've turned their own nervous systems into broadcast equipment. It's art as infection. The corps call it unlicensed neural transmission. The performers call it communion.

The residential character survived too, though transformed. Upturn is still where the city's misfits wash up — people too strange for the Gray Zone's tight-knit conformity, too broke for the Core, too analog for the Circuit. The old single-room-occupancy hotels now function as vertical communes, their residents sharing generators, food prep, and a collective commitment to being left alone. The lakefront blocks that flood during storms have been surrendered to the water, their lower floors converted to aquaculture tanks that feed the district. Mental health services — never adequate in old Uptown, criminally absent in Meridian — are provided by a network of unlicensed counselors and AI therapy programs running on donated server space. The need is enormous. The resources are not.

Upturn sits on the knife edge between revival and collapse. Every season, another venue reopens. Every season, another building fails a structural assessment that nobody conducts because nobody official cares. The district has an energy that's part creative renaissance, part hospice — the desperate brightness of people making art because the alternative is despair. Kyle comes here when he needs to remember that there's more to Meridian than contracts and chrome. The shows at the Aragon can make you weep, if you're open to it. Most of Kyle's work doesn't leave room for that kind of openness, which is exactly why he needs it.

sights: The Aragon's cracked Moorish facade lit from within by shifting neural-reactive light installations
Street performers broadcasting emotional states through jury-rigged neural transmitters, passersby stopping as feelings wash over them
Aquaculture tanks glowing green in flooded ground floors, fish shadows moving behind dirty glass
Hand-painted venue posters layered decades deep on every available wall surface
The Riviera's marquee, half its letters missing, still spelling out tonight's unlicensed show
Commune residents on fire escapes, sharing meals and cigarettes and watching the lakefront darken
sounds: Music — always music. Live drums from a basement rehearsal, synth drones from a rooftop installation, someone singing in a language that might not exist yet
The hum of neural broadcast equipment warming up before a show — a subsonic vibration you feel in your teeth
Lake waves hitting the flooded lower blocks, a rhythm the musicians have learned to play against
Applause — real applause, from real hands, which sounds different from anything a neural feed can simulate
The creak of old theater seats in the Aragon, designed for a city that doesn't exist anymore
smells: Greasepaint and ozone — the smell of performance in the neural age
Aquaculture tanks — wet vegetation and fish, not unpleasant, just biological
Old building interiors — dust, aged wood, the ghost scent of a century of cigarette smoke baked into plaster
Street food from the vendors who set up outside venues before shows, capitalizing on the crowd
Lake air from the flooded eastern blocks, cleaner here than in Rogers Reef
atmosphere.feel: Manic. Upturn vibrates between euphoria and exhaustion with nothing in between. The shows are transcendent. The mornings after are brutal. Everyone here is creating something or recovering from creating something, and the line between art and breakdown is drawn in pencil and erased frequently. It feels like the last party in a building that's being condemned — joyful, desperate, and absolutely essential.

demographics: Roughly 20,000 residents, heavily skewed toward Tier 1 and untier-ed. High population of artists, performers, unlicensed neural technicians, and the marginally housed. Significant mental health needs across the population. The most transient district in northern Meridian — people flow through Upturn constantly, staying for a season or a decade.
economy: Neural entertainment performances, experience-chip production, aquaculture, unlicensed therapy services, and the gray-market creative economy. The Aragon alone generates enough foot traffic to support a surrounding ecosystem of food vendors, augment-cosmetics artists, and stimulant dealers.
power_structure: The Venue Collective — operators of the Aragon, the Riviera, and six smaller performance spaces — functions as Upturn's de facto government. Decisions are made by consensus, which means slowly, loudly, and with dramatic walkouts. No corporate presence. No formal law enforcement.
dangers: Neural broadcast exposure — unlicensed transmissions can overwhelm unprepared implants, causing seizures or emotional flooding
Structural failure in the older venue buildings — the Aragon's balcony has been condemned and reopened four times
Exploitation of vulnerable populations — Upturn's mentally ill and marginally housed are targets for predatory augment dealers
Stimulant addiction fueled by the performance economy's demand for constant creative output
Flooding in the eastern blocks during storms — worse than the Rinse and less predictable
Experience-chip addiction — some of the content produced here is designed to be psychologically habit-forming
opportunities: Neural entertainment experiences unavailable anywhere else in Meridian — art that rewrites your emotional state
The creative community's network — performers, writers, and experience-chip artists who know people everywhere
Aquaculture products — fresh fish in a city that mostly eats synth-protein is a valuable commodity
Information exchange at venues — shows are also social gatherings where deals are made and secrets traded
Unlicensed therapy — the AI counseling programs here are better than nothing, and for many residents, they're the only option
story_hooks: A neural performer at the Aragon discovers she can transmit specific memories — not emotions, memories — through her broadcast equipment. Someone else's memories. She doesn't know whose, and they're getting darker
The Venue Collective receives an anonymous offer to buy the Aragon and convert it to a licensed corporate entertainment space. The offer is generous. The alternative is implied arson.

An experience-chip circulating in Upturn contains a hidden data payload — someone is using the entertainment distribution network to smuggle information, and the content of that information could destabilize Axiom's grip on the northern districts
frequented_by: Performers and neural broadcast artists from across Meridian
Audience members willing to travel for experiences the corporate feeds can't provide
The marginally housed seeking community and cheap accommodation
Experience-chip dealers and distributors working the venue circuit
People in crisis — Upturn's unlicensed counselors are often the last stop before Old Harbor
